tier_reason: The repository publishes no speed numbers (README and doc/benchmarking.md describe density and tooling only), and the only numbers found are third-party and show jpegli slower than libjpeg-turbo at decode (oximg issue #61), so there is no measured speed win and the entry stays D. The repo does ship a harness that could measure it (tools/benchmark/benchmark_xl with benchmark_codec_jpeg.cc), but it has no published results.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No speed advantage over libjpeg-turbo is claimed by the repository. Google's announcement blog post (blocked here; search snippet only) says Jpegli's coding speed is 'comparable to traditional approaches, such as libjpeg-turbo and MozJPEG', with no numbers. Third-party oximg issue #61 (Zen 4, 512 px, q80) states that jpegli decodes 1.6-2.0x slower than libjpeg-turbo. Its encode table has mozjpeg trellis at 10316 us against jpegli at 1812-1912 us (progressive 8-scan, 4:4:4, adaptive quantization on) and 534-546 us (upstream baseline, 4:2:0, AQ off), so jpegli encodes about 5.4-5.7x faster than mozjpeg trellis (derived from page data). The issue gives no jpegli versus libjpeg-turbo encode timing.
corrections.caveats: No speed numbers in the repository, so tier D (notable: Google project, 407 stars, libjpeg62 API/ABI drop-in with cjpegli/djpegli tools). The repo has a harness that could produce numbers but publishes none: tools/benchmark/benchmark_xl with benchmark_codec_jpeg.cc times the linked libjpeg encoder and decoder by default and jpegli with the enc-jpegli/dec-jpegli options, and reports E MP/s and D MP/s. Google's announcement blog post (opensource.googleblog.com, blocked here) is known only from a search snippet ('coding speed comparable to traditional approaches, such as libjpeg-turbo and MozJPEG', no numbers). The arXiv paper 'Users prefer Jpegli over same-sized libjpeg-turbo or MozJPEG' (2403.18589, blocked) is a subjective-quality study. The only numbers are third-party and point the other way. oximg issue #61 (opened 2026-10-01, a proposal to change oximg's jpegli encoder defaults; Zen 4, 512 px, q80) says in its out-of-scope section that jpegli decodes 1.6-2.0x slower than libjpeg-turbo, with no methodology shown for that figure. Its encode table compares jpegli configurations with oximg's current jpegli setup (jpegli-sys 0.10.2, progressive 8-scan, 4:4:4, AQ on: 1812-1912 us; baseline 4:4:4 AQ off: 960-976 us, -12.1% server cycles; upstream commit 031a0077 baseline 4:2:0 AQ off: 534-546 us, -17.3%) plus mozjpeg trellis at 10316 us. It has no libjpeg-turbo encode timing. Being faster than mozjpeg's trellis mode is not a win over the category baseline (libjpeg-turbo), and trellis quantization does different, slower work. Encode cost depends heavily on settings (progressive scans, subsampling, adaptive quantization). The '+2.6% CPU and +10% bytes' figures in the search record were not found in this verifier's reading of issue #61; oximg issue #64 and sharp issue #4018 cited by the search agent were not rechecked. A PATENTS file adds a Google patent grant (JPEG XL wording). Treat as a density and quality reference, not a speed win.

tier_reason: The project claims no speed win and its own README-mozilla.txt says it is considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo at compressing with default settings; the only third-party numbers (a 2014-era gist, oximg issue #61) also show it slower, so there are no numbers for any speed advantage and the entry stays D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No speed advantage claimed. README-mozilla.txt: 'When the default settings are used, mozjpeg is considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo or even libjpeg at compressing images. Thus, it is not generally suitable for real-time compression.' Its performance is described as highly asymmetric (compression much slower than decompression). Third-party numbers also show it slower: sergejmueller's gist (mozjpeg 2.0, 'jpegtran -copy none -progressive', 7 images) has 0.389-0.846 s against libjpeg-turbo's 0.164-0.441 s, about 2.3x slower on average for files 1.18% smaller; oximg issue #61 (Zen 4, 512 px, q80) has mozjpeg trellis at 10316 us per encode against jpegli at 1812-1912 us. With its extensions disabled it behaves exactly like libjpeg-turbo (README.md), so its decoder is libjpeg-turbo's.
corrections.caveats: No speed-win numbers anywhere, so tier D (notable: 5.7k stars, 435 forks, widely deployed in web image pipelines). It is a size-efficiency encoder (trellis quantization, optimized Huffman tables, progressive scans with jpegrescan-style scan optimization), and its own docs say it is considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo at compression with default settings. Third-party numbers agree but lack methodology: the sergejmueller gist (jpegtran -progressive with mozjpeg 2.0, 7 images, no hardware or libjpeg-turbo version stated, last updated 2019-11-14) shows about 2.3x slower lossless transcoding for 1.18% smaller files; oximg issue #61 (Zen 4, 512 px, q80, no build details) shows mozjpeg trellis at 10316 us per image, about 5.4-5.7x jpegli's progressive encode (derived from page data). libjpeg-turbo's own mozjpeg comparison page (libjpeg-turbo.org/About/Mozjpeg) is blocked here and was not read. It is a fork of libjpeg-turbo, and with its extensions disabled it behaves exactly like libjpeg-turbo, so decode speed is libjpeg-turbo's. Versions: the GitHub releases page lists v4.1.1 ('Updated to libjpeg-turbo 2.1.3', 15 Aug, year not shown) as the latest tagged release, while master's ChangeLog.md tops out at the inherited libjpeg-turbo 3.0.5 entry (master merged libjpeg-turbo 3.0.x in January 2025); speed figures in that ChangeLog are libjpeg-turbo's, not mozjpeg's. Last commit 2025-06-23 (Fix PNG detection in CMake), so maintenance is stale. License: IJG for the libjpeg API library, BSD-3-Clause for TurboJPEG and the build system, zlib for SIMD code (LICENSE.md). Useful as the baseline of the listed mozjpeg-rs and as a reference for the speed cost of trellis quantization.
